name: Eight values
why: [3, 9, 10, 15, 27, 38, 43, 82]. If values are missing, the merge forgets to copy what is left of one list after the other runs out.

name: Odd length
why: Halves of 2 and 3. If you get an endless recursion, the split must make both parts strictly shorter: mid = len(a) // 2 with a base case for length 0 and 1.

name: Repeats
why: [1, 1, 2, 2, 2]. If a value is missing or appears too often, the merge drops or copies a value on a tie: take exactly one value per pass, and copy what is left of both lists at the end.

name: Empty and one
why: Base cases: a list of 0 or 1 values is already sorted. Return a copy.

name: Negative values
why: [-5, -5, -1, 0, 3]. Merge sort only compares values, so negative values need nothing special. If they come out in the wrong place, the code sorts by something other than the value itself, such as abs(x) or str(x).

name: Input not changed
why: Return a new sorted list and leave a as it was.

name: 100,000 values
expr: (lambda r: [len(r), all(r[i] <= r[i + 1] for i in range(len(r) - 1)), r[:3], r[-3:]])(merge_sort(args[0]))
show: 100,000 values; [length, sorted?, first three, last three]
why: n log n is about 1.7 million steps. If this timed out, the merge may use pop(0), which is O(n) each time; use two indexes instead.
